paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Copenhagen interpretation is a family of ideas about what quantum mechanics really means, rooted in work by Niels Bohr, Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and others. Quantum mechanics does not sit easily with everyday language and experience, and even the people who built it often found it strange. The Copenhagen ideas offer one way to think about how the theory's mathematics connects to the physical world.

paragraphs.heading: The core ideas
paragraphs.text: Most versions share a few features. Quantum mechanics is taken to be indeterministic at its root, and it gives probabilities worked out with the Born rule, which turns a system's wave function into odds for each measurement result. Then there is complementarity: some pairs of properties of an object cannot all be observed or measured at once. Measuring an object is also irreversible, and nothing can be called true of it except what its measurement shows.

paragraphs.heading: The lab set-up matters
paragraphs.text: To talk about a particular property of a system, you have to picture that system inside a specific laboratory arrangement. Quantities tied to arrangements that exclude one another cannot be predicted together. Yet you still need several such experiments to describe the system fully. The readings that measuring devices give are basically classical and should be put in ordinary language, a point Bohr pressed hard and Heisenberg accepted.

paragraphs.heading: Born in the 1920s
paragraphs.text: The ideas took shape between 1925 and 1927. In 1925 Heisenberg described electrons using only quantities that could be observed, which for him meant the frequencies of light that atoms absorb and emit. Max Born saw that in this theory, position and momentum become matrices: mathematical objects that multiply like numbers, except that the order of multiplying changes the answer. When Erwin Schrödinger wrote an equation treating the electron as a wave, Born found that its wave function worked best as a tool for calculating probabilities.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: The name points to Copenhagen, the city where Bohr and Heisenberg worked. The label itself seems to have come from Heisenberg around 1955, while he was attacking rival interpretations such as David Bohm's. Before his book went on sale, Heisenberg privately regretted the term, because it implied that other interpretations existed, and he judged those to be nonsense. In 1960 Léon Rosenfeld, a close collaborator of Bohr, called it an ambiguous expression and proposed dropping it, but the name spread widely anyway.

paragraphs.heading: Many versions, still taught
paragraphs.text: There is no single official statement of the view. Bohr and Heisenberg wrote things that clash on several key issues, and Bohr kept his distance from what he saw as Heisenberg's more subjective reading. Asher Peres noted that different authors present very different, even opposite, views under the same name, and David Mermin spoke of its many flavors. Critics have objected to the sudden, random nature of measurement and to the trouble of saying what counts as a measuring device. Even so, it remains one of the most commonly taught interpretations.
